gefallen.et: From Middle High German gevallen, from Old High German gifallan. Equivalent to ge- (expressing the terminative aspect) + fallen.

s: Niemand konnte ihn hier vermuten, er hatte das Gefühl vollkommener Sicherheit, von keiner Seite drohte irgendwelche Gefahr.
Nobody could suppose him to be here, he had the feeling of complete security, from no side did any danger threaten him.
Gefahr.et: From Middle High German gevāre, gevære, from Old High German fāra, from Proto-Germanic *fērō. Cognate with English fear and Dutch gevaar.

Gefäß.et: From Middle High German gevǣȥe, from Old High German givāȥi; by surface analysis, ge- + fassen. Cognate with Plautdietsch Jefäss.

Gefährte.et: From Middle High German geverte, from Old High German giferto (“companion, he who travels with someone”), from Proto-West Germanic *gafardijō. By surface analysis, ge- + Fahrt + -e. Cognate with Old Dutch geferdi, Middle Low German gevērde. Also related with O…

s: companion (female, or sexless but feminine), friend (female, or sexless but feminine)
Sie war meine Gefährtin für viele Jahre.
She was my companion for many years.

gefangen.et: From Middle High German gefangen, gevangen, from Old High German gifangan, from Proto-West Germanic *gafangan, past participle of *fą̄han, equivalent to ge- + fangen. Cognate with Middle Low German gevangen, Dutch gevangen.

s: Das Gefängnis, das heute in Deutschland nicht mehr strafen sondern bessern und erziehen soll, ist damit sozusagen zum Lazarett der bürgerlichen Ordnung avanciert.
The prison, which today in Germany is not supposed to punish anymore but to better and educate, has thereby advanced to the military hospital of the bourgeois order, so to speak.
to be sentenced to 10 years in prison.
Gefängnis.et: From Middle High German (ge)vancnisse, (ge)vencnisse (“capture, captivity”), since 15th century for the place of the captivity, equivalent to gefangen (“caught”) + -nis. More at fangen (“to catch”). Cognate with Dutch gevangenis.

s: favor, favour (UK) (a deed in which help is voluntarily provided)
Gefallen.et: From earlier Gefalle, from Middle High German geval, equivalent to a deverbal of gefallen (compare Fall). Originally a strong noun, but seemingly shifting to a weak paradigm before regularizing back into its modern, strong form by adapting the oblique weak end…

Gefährt.et: From Middle High German geverte (“way, ride, walk, behaviour”), from Old High German *giferti (attested as giverte, etc.), from faran, whence modern fahren. The contemporary sense (17th c.) after cognate Middle Low German gevērde.
